rv.q: Margulies brings a warm, conversational ease to the role that makes you feel as if you're sitting across from her at a coffee shop, listening to her recount the most important chapters of her life.

If nothing else, Delia Ephron’s autobiographical romantic comedy Left on Tenth, opening tonight on Broadway, proves that Ephron, like her late sister Nora, can find the feel-good in even the most unlikely places.

At other times, you might well think that you could be lying in bed and reading the justly well-regarded source memoir and getting much the same benefits from the experience without paying for a theater ticket.
Though the show is beautifully acted and staged, it feels more like a gentle memorial service than a fully realized theatrical experience.
You are in for an evening that is altogether too pleasant for its own good.
But the mangled tone, laughless jokes and emotional fakery are impossible to look beyond.
The thrill-free theatrical mounting of Delia Ephron's memoir is a disappointing regurgitation of its source material.
That drama does not translate, alas, to this attenuated theatrical version.
It is a diverting evening in the theater although don’t expect any insights or revelations.
While appealing to die-hard romcom fans, Left on Tenth doesn’t fulfill the potential of its alluring premise.
Delia Ephron’s Left on Tenth is a delightful and moving journey of grief and love that shines in moments but struggles to find its footing on stage.
As it stands, “Left on Tenth” feels like watching a rom-com with two extremely good-looking middle-aged people.
By the end of the evening, you’ll have come to very much like Delia Ephron.
Ephron’s experience is powerful and affecting, but some stories simply don’t translate from the page to the stage.

But its presentation feels too-cute and lightly done on stage, particularly when it comes to a moment—with Delia very ill, and Peter ministering to her—that seems tailor-made to ask more of him as a character.
It's hard not to feel like Ephron had copy/pasted a first-person memoir into monologue format and called it a play.
What I’m sure is a moving, personal and vulnerable novel loses much in its translation to the stage; posing the question: Why does this need to be theater?
But despite its very best intentions, the play is frustratingly surface level, rarely delving beyond Hallmark card sentiments about taking the good with the bad.
Ephron’s memoir just didn’t translate well to the stage.
“Left on Tenth” captures perfectly the tedium of being in a hospital, for both the patient and the visitor.
Left on Tenth is a journey worth taking, utterly deserving of the spotlight it stands in.
This dynamic turn of events, although sad on a superficial level, never seems to really hit all that hard within this play.
Instead of testing this young couple’s relationship, though, the hospital-set final sections of the play merely test our patience.
As staged with beautiful actors in beautiful settings, even its most serious scenes partake of a rom-com glow that inoculates you against feeling the curse of reality even in a true story.

cn.t: Critics find this memoir adaptation charming but dramatically inert, with Margulies' warm performance unable to overcome a theatrical structure that fails to translate the source material's emotional depth to the stage.

sg.ra: JEJ is one of Broadway's smallest houses (1,063-1,092 seats across sources) and seats 101-112 in Center Orch rows AA-A put you almost nose-to-stage; SeatPlan and Headout both name seats 105-109 in AA-A as the single best spots. Mezz overhang doesn't bite until Row J, so Center Orch stays clean of ceiling cutoff all the way back to Row I.

SeatPlan explicitly calls out 'Rows E to J in the Center Orchestra are cheaper than premium with a good view,' and because JEJ's auditorium is unusually compact even Row J sits closer to the stage than mid-orch in bigger Shubert houses. This is the sweet spot before the Mezz overhang obscures the top of the stage (SeatPlan: cuts in after Row O; TickPick: overhang begins Row J but worsens deeper).

sg.vl: Overview pick with an elevated head-on
sg.ra: JEJ Mezz is one of Broadway's smallest (264-275 seats) and sits directly above the stage per SeatPlan: 'every row facing directly above the stage.' SeatPlan notes the Balcony overhang at Mezz Row B 'doesn't affect views' and the railing height doesn't obstruct (TickPick). Good rake means heads-in-front is a non-issue. AVFMS April 2024: 'View was fantastic, person in front didn't obstruct my view.'

sg.vl: Underrated value if you skew center
sg.ra: Unusual for Broadway, TickPick explicitly states JEJ 'does not have obstructed view seats on the sides of the orchestra and mezzanine' thanks to the small footprint and no pillars. But SeatPlan warns double-digit seats at the far side and Boxes above 16 are angled with stage right partially obstructed, so you want the low-numbered seats closer to center aisle.
sg.rr: L Mezz A-G odd 1-25; R Mezz A-G even 2-26; plus 24 box seats

sg.vl: Cheapest tier, steepest price in comfort
sg.ra: SeatPlan: Balcony is 'very steep and cramped compared to the lower two seating areas,' ~2 steps down per row with three flights of stairs (Shubert: 55 steps total or elevator post-renovation). SeatPlan flags Row H as 'isn't as well-raked as the rest of the section,' so the back row both loses rake AND inherits the steep climb. JEJ balcony is unusually high — Shubert's own description puts it behind Row F entrance.
sg.rr: A-G (L/R) / A-H (Center); 283 seats plus 12 box seats
